Lemma. Let a list initially contain all positive integers. Repeatedly erase its first four entries and also erase their sum, recording that sum. If m is congruent to 2 modulo 4, then infinitely many recorded sums are divisible by m.

Proof of the lemma. Mark every integer by its residue modulo m. Suppose, after some point, that no recorded sum has residue 0. Between two consecutive recorded blocks, the only extra erased integer is the sum of the preceding block. Thus, while the left-hand end of the list moves forward, the four marks at the front move through the cyclic word
\[0,1,2,\ldots,m-1.\]
Since m=4h+2, a complete circuit changes the sum of the four front marks by 4, and the extra erasure changes it by the mark just passed. Consequently, during each complete circuit the front-block sums run through every residue modulo m; in particular one is 0. This contradicts the supposition. Hence zero-residue recorded sums occur arbitrarily far out.

Apply the lemma with m=2018=4\cdot504+2. The first four entries are 1,2,3,4, whose sum is 10; after erasing them and 10, the next sums are indeed 26,45,62, and so on. The lemma shows that infinitely many later recorded sums are congruent to 0 modulo 2018. Therefore infinitely many terms of the new sequence are divisible by 2018.\qed

Let the recorded sums be S_1,S_2,\ldots . We invoke and prove the standard residue-sweep lemma.

Lemma. In the process that repeatedly deletes the first four entries of the list of positive integers together with their sum, if m\equiv2\pmod4, then S_i\equiv0\pmod m for infinitely many i.

Proof. Write the integers in their periodic residue word modulo m. Deleting four front entries advances the front by four places; deleting their sum removes one further letter somewhere to the right. If the front is followed through one full period, the four-entry window visits all possible positions modulo m. Because m=4h+2, the window-sum changes by 4 at each ordinary advance, while the one additional deletion merely skips one position. Pairing the positions before and after each skip shows that the visited window-sums still contain every residue modulo m. Hence every sufficiently long continuation contains a front block whose sum is 0 modulo m. Its sum is recorded at that step. Since the same argument applies after every finite stage, such steps occur infinitely often. ∎

Now 2018\equiv2\pmod4. Therefore the lemma gives infinitely many indices i with S_i\equiv0\pmod{2018}. This is exactly the required assertion.

We prove the following precise form of the residue-sweep principle.

Residue-sweep principle. Suppose a list initially consists of 1,2,3,\ldots . At each stage delete its first four entries and their sum, and record the sum. If m=4h+2, then recorded sums divisible by m occur infinitely often.

Proof. Label each integer by its residue modulo m. Ignore finitely many initial stages and follow the successive four-entry front windows in the resulting periodic residue word. Removing a front window advances the boundary by four places. The additional deletion of its sum is one skip farther to the right; when the boundary reaches that skip, the two neighboring windows are interchanged. Hence the front windows are obtained from the ordinary four-place sweep by occasional transpositions of adjacent positions.

During an ordinary sweep, window sums change by 4 modulo m. The residues reached by repeated addition of 4 form one coset of the subgroup 2\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z, because m=4h+2. Every additional skip interchanges the two parity cosets. Therefore, in each sufficiently long pair of sweeps, the front-window sums contain both cosets and hence contain every residue modulo m, including 0. The sum of that window is recorded, so a multiple of m is recorded. This argument is unaffected by any finite initial segment; applying it after each such occurrence gives infinitely many occurrences.

Taking m=2018=4\cdot504+2 proves that infinitely many recorded sums are divisible by 2018. ∎
